questions.q: Under Section 5 of the Transfer of Property Act, "transfer of property" refers to an act by which a living person conveys property to:
o: Only a government entity
One or more other living persons, or to himself, or to himself and one or more other living persons
Only a deceased person's estate
Only a minor
questions.src: Section 5 defines transfer broadly, covering conveyance to other living persons or even to oneself, with "living person" including companies/associations.

questions.q: Under Section 6, which of the following is generally NOT transferable?
o: A house owned outright
The chance of an heir-apparent succeeding to an estate (spes successionis)
A registered mortgage interest
A leasehold interest
questions.src: Spes successionis (a mere expectancy of future inheritance) is explicitly excluded from transferability under Section 6, being too uncertain/contingent a "right" to transfer.

questions.q: Under Section 10, a condition ABSOLUTELY restraining a transferee from ever parting with their interest in transferred property is:
o: Always valid and fully enforceable
VOID to the extent of the restraint, reflecting the law's general policy favouring free alienability
Valid only if in writing
Only applicable to movable property
questions.src: Section 10 voids absolute restraints on alienation, subject to narrow exceptions, protecting the general principle that property should remain freely transferable.

questions.q: A "Vested Interest," as distinguished from a "Contingent Interest," is characterised by:
o: An incomplete title dependent on an uncertain future event
A COMPLETE title immediately upon transfer, even if enjoyment/possession is postponed
Never being heritable under any circumstances
Requiring court approval to exist
questions.src: A vested interest gives the transferee complete, present title immediately, distinguishing it from a contingent interest's incomplete, event-dependent title.

questions.q: Under Section 14 (Rule Against Perpetuity), vesting of a future interest cannot be postponed beyond:
o: A fixed period of 5 years regardless of circumstances
A life in being at the date of transfer, PLUS the minority of the ultimate beneficiary
Indefinitely, with no limit whatsoever
Exactly 100 years in every case
questions.src: This is the precise Section 14 formula — life in being plus minority (18 years) of the ultimate beneficiary — that must be stated exactly, not approximated.

questions.q: Under Section 13, a transfer for the benefit of an UNBORN PERSON requires that the interest given to that unborn person:
o: May be limited to a partial/life interest only
Must extend to the WHOLE of the transferor's remaining interest in the property, not merely a limited interest
Can never be made under any circumstances
Requires the unborn person to already exist at the time of transfer
questions.src: Section 13 mandates the unborn person receive the entire remaining interest (an absolute interest), preventing indefinite generational tie-up through successive limited interests.

questions.q: The Doctrine of Election under Section 35 applies when a person, professing to transfer property they do NOT own, in the SAME transaction:
o: Grants no benefit to the real owner at all
Confers a benefit on the REAL OWNER of that property, who must then elect to confirm the transfer or reject it and give up the benefit
Automatically transfers full ownership without any choice
Applies only to movable property
questions.src: The real owner must choose consistently — either accept the whole transaction (transfer plus benefit) or reject the whole (keep the property, forgo the benefit) — reflecting the "cannot approbate and reprobate" principle.

questions.q: Under Section 54, a "Sale" of tangible immovable property valued at Rs. 100 or more requires:
o: No formal requirements whatsoever
A REGISTERED INSTRUMENT
Only an oral agreement between the parties
Approval from a magistrate
questions.src: Section 54 mandates registration for sale of tangible immovable property valued Rs. 100 or more, and for any transfer of intangible property regardless of value.

questions.q: A mere CONTRACT for sale (agreement to sell), as distinguished from a completed sale, generally:
o: Immediately transfers full ownership to the buyer
Does NOT, by itself, create any interest in or charge on the property
Requires no registration under any circumstances
Is identical in legal effect to a completed sale
questions.src: An agreement to sell is merely a contract; ownership passes only upon actual completion of the sale (registration where required), not upon the agreement alone.

questions.q: Under Section 58, a "Mortgage" is best described as:
o: A complete, absolute transfer of full ownership
The transfer of an INTEREST in specific immovable property, to secure payment of money advanced/to be advanced or performance of a pecuniary engagement
A form of lease with no security purpose
A gift with a repayment condition
questions.src: A mortgage transfers only an interest (as security), not full ownership — the mortgagor retains ownership subject to the mortgagee's security interest.

questions.q: A "Usufructuary Mortgage" is characterised by:
o: The mortgagor retaining possession throughout
The mortgagor DELIVERING POSSESSION to the mortgagee, who retains it and receives rents/profits in lieu of interest/principal until repayment
An absolute sale with no right of redemption
Requiring no delivery of possession under any circumstances
questions.src: Usufructuary mortgages specifically involve transfer of possession to the mortgagee, who is compensated through the property's rents/profits rather than direct interest payments.

questions.q: A "Charge" under Section 100, as distinguished from a "Mortgage," is characterised by:
o: Always transferring a full interest in the property
NOT involving any transfer of an actual interest in the property, merely making it security for payment
Requiring exactly the same formalities as a mortgage in every case
Being identical in legal effect to a mortgage
questions.src: The essential distinguishing feature of a charge is the absence of any transfer of interest — unlike a mortgage, which does transfer an interest as security.

questions.q: Under Section 105, a "Lease" is defined as a transfer of:
o: Full ownership of the property permanently
A RIGHT TO ENJOY immovable property for a certain time or in perpetuity, in consideration of a price/rent
Only movable property
A mere licence to visit the property occasionally
questions.src: A lease transfers a genuine right to enjoy the property (an actual interest), distinguishing it from a mere licence.

questions.q: A "Lease," as distinguished from a "Licence," transfers:
o: No interest whatsoever, exactly like a licence
An actual, transferable INTEREST in the property, enforceable against the world; a licence merely grants personal permission with no such interest
Only a right to sue for damages
Identical rights to both parties in every respect
questions.src: This is one of the most heavily tested distinctions — a lease creates a genuine property interest, while a licence is merely personal permission, generally revocable and not binding on subsequent owners.

questions.q: Under Section 106, in the absence of a written contract or local usage, a lease for AGRICULTURAL or MANUFACTURING purposes is deemed a lease:
o: From month to month, terminable by 15 days' notice
From year to year, terminable by 6 months' notice
For a fixed 99-year term automatically
That can never be terminated
questions.src: Agricultural/manufacturing leases default to a year-to-year term with 6 months' notice, distinguishing them from the month-to-month default (15 days' notice) for other purposes.

questions.q: Under Section 122, a "Gift" is defined as a transfer of EXISTING property made:
o: For substantial consideration
VOLUNTARILY and WITHOUT CONSIDERATION, accepted by the donee during the donor's lifetime
Only after the donor's death
Only to family members
questions.src: Gift requires voluntariness, absence of consideration, and crucially, acceptance by the donee during the donor's lifetime — acceptance after death is invalid.

questions.q: A gift of IMMOVABLE property, under Section 123, must generally be effected by:
o: A mere oral declaration with no other formality
A REGISTERED INSTRUMENT, signed by/on behalf of the donor and attested by at least TWO witnesses
Simply handing over possession with no documentation
A verbal promise witnessed by one person
questions.src: Section 123 mandates formal registration and attestation by two witnesses for a valid gift of immovable property.

questions.q: Under Section 52 (Doctrine of Lis Pendens), a property that is the subject of a PENDING, NON-COLLUSIVE suit:
o: Can be freely transferred with no legal consequence whatsoever
Cannot be transferred by a party to the suit so as to affect the other party's rights, except with court authority
Must always be transferred to the court itself
Automatically becomes government property
questions.src: Section 52 subjects any transfer during pending litigation to the outcome of that litigation, protecting the integrity of the judicial process.

questions.q: In Bellamy v. Sabine (1857), the court held that the Doctrine of Lis Pendens is founded on:
o: Whether the purchaser had actual notice of the pending litigation
The necessity that legal proceedings must be capable of running their course to a binding conclusion, without being defeated by transfers during litigation
The purchaser's financial capacity
The age of the property being litigated
questions.src: Bellamy v. Sabine established that lis pendens does not depend on notice — its foundation is the broader necessity of preserving the effectiveness of litigation.

questions.q: Under Section 53A (Doctrine of Part Performance), a transferee who has taken possession in part performance of a written contract, and is ready/willing to perform their obligations, is protected by:
o: Gaining an independent right to sue for full ownership
Being shielded from the transferor enforcing rights INCONSISTENT with the contract's terms, despite formal transfer not being completed — a purely DEFENSIVE protection
Automatically becoming the registered owner
No protection whatsoever
questions.src: Part Performance operates as "a shield, not a sword" — purely defensive, protecting existing possession without conferring an independent affirmative right of action.

questions.q: In Mohd. Musa v. Aghor Kumar Ganguli (1914), the Privy Council held that the equitable Doctrine of Part Performance:
o: Has never applied in India under any circumstances
Was applicable in India even BEFORE its formal statutory codification via Section 53A (inserted in 1929)
Only applies to movable property
Requires the property to be registered before any protection can arise
questions.src: This Privy Council ruling recognised Part Performance as applicable in India through equity, predating the Act's formal 1929 amendment inserting Section 53A.

questions.q: Section 53A generally does NOT apply where the underlying agreement to transfer property is:
o: In writing with reasonably certain terms
Purely ORAL, with no signed writing setting out the essential terms
Signed by both parties
For a small parcel of land
questions.src: Settled case law (e.g., Kalawati Tripathi and similar rulings) confirms Section 53A requires a signed writing; purely oral agreements fall outside its protection.

questions.q: Under Section 118, an "Exchange" occurs when two persons mutually transfer ownership of one thing for another, where:
o: Both things being exchanged must always be money
NEITHER thing (or not both things) is money only
Only one party needs to actually transfer anything
The transaction must always involve immovable property exclusively
questions.src: Exchange specifically excludes transactions where both things exchanged are purely money (which would simply be a sale/payment, not an exchange).

questions.q: The Doctrine of Election is often summarised by the maxim that a person cannot:
o: Ever accept any benefit under any document
APPROBATE and REPROBATE the same instrument — accept its benefit while rejecting its burden
Transfer property to an unborn person under any circumstances
Enter into more than one contract at a time
questions.src: This maxim captures the Doctrine of Election's core logic — consistency is required; a person must either accept or reject the whole transaction, not selectively take the favourable parts.

questions.q: Under Section 9, a transfer of property may generally be made WITHOUT WRITING:
o: In every case without exception
In every case EXCEPT where writing is expressly required by law (e.g., sales above Rs. 100, most mortgages, gifts of immovable property, leases over one year)
Only for movable property under Rs. 10
Only with a magistrate's prior permission
questions.src: Section 9 permits oral transfers generally, but numerous specific provisions throughout the Act carve out categories requiring written, registered instruments.
